appraisal_events.evidence: certaines femmes, comme Mme de Franquetot, semblaient ne pas pouvoir retirer complètement leur robe restée accrochée à la pierre du caveau... elles tremblaient et leurs doigts ne pouvaient rien retenir
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator singles Mme de Franquetot out as the named instance of a body visibly failing, caught in a curve poised between life and death, a direct image of physical and existential diminishment.

appraisal_events.evidence: tout concourait chez lui à donner une impression nouvelle de majesté fatale... ma première pensée fut de le féliciter non d'avoir été promu colonel, mais d'être si bien en colonel
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator is struck into admiration by how age has recast Beausergent into a figure of doge-like majesty worthy of an Old Master portrait, but the elevation is immediately undercut by the ironic observation that this is really a convincing disguise borrowed from his father, so the positive movement is genuine yet layered with irony rather than purely endorsed.

status_effects.explanation: She is presented as the concrete, named example of decrepitude and imminent death within this passage's catalogue of aged guests.

His transformed appearance is described with terms of grandeur and artistic distinction, giving a local positive movement, though the framing as pathological 'disguise' tempers how far it is elevated.

ambiguities: The admiring description of the marquis de Beausergent ('majesté fatale', comparison to Mantegna/Michelangelo studies) is intertwined with an ironic register, since the transformation is explicitly attributed to arteriosclerosis and the narrator's impulse is only to congratulate him on looking convincingly disguised as a colonel rather than on any real distinction; the elevation is therefore not straightforwardly endorsed.
